name: Ticket & Event Scams
summary: Tickets to sold-out events are sold on social media and resale groups, either duplicated, already used, or entirely fictional.

typicalLoss.note: Losses spike around major concerts, rugby and cricket fixtures and festivals.

targets: Young people buying through social media

howItWorks.detail: The event is sold out, and the buyer is emotionally committed before any verification happens.
A profile with history, a plausible reason for selling, and a screenshot of the ticket that looks entirely real.
Payment by EFT, then a PDF or a barcode screenshot. The same barcode may be sold to twenty buyers, only the first of whom gets in.
The failure happens at the turnstile, hours after the seller has gone quiet and long past any chance of recovery.

redFlags: Payment by EFT to a personal account for a ticket.
A ticket sent as a screenshot or PDF rather than an official transfer through the ticketing platform.
The seller refuses to meet or to use an escrow or platform transfer.
Pressure created by the event being imminent.
A profile created recently, or with no mutual connections and little history.
illustrativeCase: Ahead of a sold-out stadium concert, a Facebook group seller offers four tickets at face value, sending a clear photograph of the barcodes. Six separate buyers pay R3 200 each for the same four barcodes. One group is admitted. The other five are turned away at the gate, and the seller's profile is deleted that night.
howToProtect: Only buy through the official ticketing platform's own resale or transfer function, which reissues the barcode to you.
Never accept a screenshot or PDF as proof of a valid ticket. Barcodes copy perfectly.
Pay by card or through the platform, never EFT to an individual.
Be most careful when you want it most. Desire for the event is the entire mechanism.
Verify that the ticket has been transferred into your own account before paying.
ifYouveBeenHit: Report to your bank immediately, and lodge a chargeback if you paid by card.
Report the seller and listing to the platform and the group administrators.
Open a SAPS case, ideally grouped with other victims of the same seller.
Contact the event organiser, who sometimes flags duplicated barcodes and occasionally assists.

faqs.q: Can a ticket barcode be checked before the event?
faqs.a: Usually not by a buyer, which is precisely the gap this scam exploits. The only real protection is an official transfer into your own account.

faqs.q: The seller had a real-looking profile with photos.
faqs.a: Profiles are bought, stolen or aged deliberately. Profile appearance is not verification.
